examples.whatToDo: Phrase the offer as accepting responsibility for a bad night, not as pleading guilty to a charge his mother will hear named and carry to church on Sunday.
examples.whyItMatters: A nineteen-year-old will fight a losing case to keep from being labeled in front of the woman who raised him. The label, not the sentence, is what he is defending. Change the label and the case settles.

examples.title: Mahalia at the Kitchen Table, Reading Joelle's Chart

planSpec.domain: a hospice nurse correcting a grown daughter who has been giving her dying father the wrong dose because she misread the chart
planSpec.audience: a hospice nurse on a home visit
planSpec.stakes: whether the daughter keeps caring for her father at home or collapses into guilt and hands him over to a facility
planSpec.requiredBeat: the nurse praises the daughter's vigilance, locates the error in the chart's handwriting rather than the daughter's care, and corrects the dose without ever making her say she was wrong

examples.scenario: Mahalia steps into the kitchen of a small Asheville house and sees, before anything, what Joelle has done well: pill cups lined up by color, a printed log of every dose, a sleeping father whose pain looks contained. Then she sees the chart. The dose is written 2.5, in handwriting cramped enough to pass for 25. Joelle has been reading 25. Mahalia thinks: I will praise the log first. I will ask whose handwriting this is. I will say the pen was unkind to a tired reader. I will not make her name what she has been doing wrong.
examples.whatToDo: Praise the daughter's care first, then place the error in the chart's bad handwriting. Recompute the dose with her, out loud, so she lands on the right number herself.
examples.whyItMatters: When a caregiver feels accused, she withdraws. The dying man then loses the person who has been most vigilant about him, and a fixable misreading becomes a permanent change in who is allowed to help.

examples.title: Romilly walks her teacher back through the parent's inbox

planSpec.domain: a high school principal handling a teacher who sent a sharply worded email to a parent that has now reached the superintendent
planSpec.audience: a principal who needs the teacher to write an apology that does not read as forced
planSpec.stakes: whether the teacher learns to write a different email next time or hardens into resentment and a union grievance
planSpec.requiredBeat: the principal walks through what the parent likely felt reading the email, lets the teacher arrive at the rewrite herself, and never makes her recant the original in writing

examples.scenario: Romilly has the printed email on her desk Friday after dismissal, the teacher sitting across from her with arms crossed. She does not ask for an apology. She reads the email aloud slowly, the way a mother might read it on her phone in a hospital break room at the end of a double shift. Then she sets the page down. 'What do you think she did with her hands when she got to the second paragraph?' The teacher is quiet. Romilly waits, and is about to ask the next question, the one that hands the rewrite back.
examples.whatToDo: Read the email back to her in the parent's voice. Ask what the parent felt at each line. Let her propose the rewrite herself, and never ask her to recant the original in writing.
examples.whyItMatters: An apology written under demand reads like one and teaches nothing. An apology that arrives because the writer has stood inside the reader's experience is what changes how the next email gets written.

questions.prompt: A bakery shift lead notices a new baker has been laminating croissants with too few folds all week. The full staff is at the bench and regulars are at the counter. What is the soundest move?
choices: Walk back to the cooler with him for a moment and frame the fix as a clarification on the recipe card.
Call the correct fold count across the bench so the whole crew hears the standard at once.
Wait until Monday's one-on-one and review every croissant photo from the week with him.
questions.explanation: The correction has to happen, but in a setting where he is not branded in front of peers. Naming a recipe-card ambiguity gives him a way to fix the work without confessing. Calling it across the bench guarantees humiliation, and waiting through Monday lets bad pastry ship for two more days.

questions.prompt: A junior developer pushed a config change that briefly took staging down. The rest of the team saw the alert. The team lead is about to address it in standup. Which opener does the most work?
choices: List the three checks the junior skipped so everyone learns from the mistake at once.
Note that the deploy guide does not flag this config as risky and ask the junior to help rewrite the section.
Skip standup mention entirely and pretend the outage never happened.
questions.explanation: Locating the gap in the deploy guide lets the junior fix the issue without being marked as the one who broke staging. Listing skipped checks publicly humiliates her and ends the lesson. Pretending nothing happened protects her face but teaches no one, including her.

questions.prompt: A dental hygienist sees a patient has been flossing in a way that is wearing his gums. He has been proudly flossing twice a day for six months. Which approach keeps him flossing?
choices: Tell him bluntly that what he has been doing is wrong and show him the recession on a mirror.
Stay quiet about the technique and just clean carefully so he does not feel criticized.
Praise the daily habit first, then show him a slightly different angle as the next step for someone already this consistent.
questions.explanation: Naming the real strength first reframes the change as an upgrade for a consistent flosser, not a verdict on him. Bluntly calling him wrong attacks pride and risks him quitting the habit. Saying nothing leaves the gum damage in place, which is its own failure of care.

questions.prompt: A site superintendent had to remove a long-tenured foreman from running the framing crew after a string of quality issues. Instead of announcing a demotion, she offered him a new role training apprentices across her three sites. He stayed. What was the load-bearing move?
choices: She built the new role around a strength he was already known for, so accepting was not the same as confessing failure.
She kept his old salary, which made the title change feel cosmetic.
She made the announcement on a Friday so the news had the weekend to settle.
questions.explanation: Handing him a role that uses a real strength gives him a story he can carry home that is not 'I was demoted'. Same pay helps but does not change how he tells the story. Friday timing is a logistical detail and would not have moved a proud man on its own.

questions.prompt: A department head pulled a senior analyst into a conference room with two HR reps and presented a written warning about her recent reports. The analyst nodded, signed, and quit two weeks later. Where did the head most likely lose her?
choices: He should have written the warning more strongly so she understood the seriousness.
The setup, two HR reps and a signed document, made the meeting feel like a sentencing and gave her no way to fix the work without first wearing the verdict.
He should have copied her teammates so they could weigh in on her reports.
questions.explanation: The room itself made the correction unrecoverable. With two witnesses and a signature line, accepting the feedback meant accepting the brand. A stronger warning compounds the problem, and looping in teammates would broadcast the humiliation she was already trying to escape.

questions.prompt: Two PTA chairs handle a volunteer who has been double-counting fundraiser receipts. Chair A reads the corrected totals aloud at the meeting. Chair B walks her through the receipt template the next afternoon. The volunteer keeps showing up only after Chair B's approach. Why?
choices: Public correction is faster and clearer, so it should have worked, but the volunteer was unusually sensitive.
Chair A's approach is better in principle but timing matters in PTA dynamics.
Chair B located the error in the template, in private, leaving the volunteer with a fix to make rather than a public stain to live down.
questions.explanation: The volunteer can take a correction in private about a template. She cannot take being publicly recast as someone who cannot count. Calling her unusually sensitive misreads the situation, and there is no version of public number-correction that respects a volunteer's pride.

questions.prompt: A small-firm partner needs a junior attorney to fix a brief that has factual errors. The brief was already shared with co-counsel. Which note to the junior best preserves both the relationship and the work?
choices: I caught a few citation issues, can you and I sit down tomorrow and tighten it before we send the revised version to co-counsel.
Your brief has errors. Please correct them today and re-send to the team with an explanation.
I will rewrite the brief myself this evening, do not worry about it, we can talk later.
questions.explanation: Framing it as joint work to tighten lets the junior fix her own errors without an audit trail of shame. A blunt directive is a public scold she will remember. Quietly rewriting it teaches her nothing and signals that her work cannot be trusted to her face.

questions.prompt: A new manager hears the phrase 'let the other person save face' and asks what it actually requires of him in practice. Which description best captures it?
choices: Avoid all corrections so the other person never feels bad.
When you must correct or move someone, give them a version of the change they can carry home without shame.
Make sure the other person admits out loud that they were wrong before you offer any kindness.
questions.explanation: The point is not to skip the correction or to extract a confession. It is to deliver the correction in a form that leaves the other person with a story they can live inside. Avoiding it lets the work suffer. Demanding admission makes the change a public defeat.

questions.prompt: A real estate broker realizes a junior agent has been pricing listings ten percent below comp for the neighborhood, costing sellers real money. The brokerage Slack channel is where most coaching happens. Where should the conversation start?
choices: In the Slack channel so the rest of the office sees the comp methodology.
In a forwarded email chain to the agent's mentor so the mentor delivers the news.
In a quiet sit-down where the broker frames the fix as a comp-pull checklist they will both use going forward.
questions.explanation: A private sit-down with a shared checklist gives the agent a tool to fix the pattern, not a public mark to wear. Slack coaching turns the lesson into a spectacle. Routing it through her mentor avoids her face but also avoids the broker's actual job, which is to coach directly.

reviewCards.front: You are about to correct someone who is clearly wrong. Before you speak, what is the one question you should ask yourself?
reviewCards.back: Not whether you are correct. Ask what this person has to carry out of the room when the conversation ends. If the answer is humiliation, they will fight the change for years. If it is a story they can live inside, they will accept it.

reviewCards.front: A junior accountant on your team has been miscoding an expense category for two weeks. The quarterly close is Friday. How do you raise it?
reviewCards.back: Pull him aside privately and locate the error in the coding guide or the system prompt, not in his judgment. Hand him the dignified exit before you press the point, so he can fix the entries without having to confess he was wrong in front of the team.

reviewCards.front: Your teenage son insists a homework answer is right. You can see it is wrong. What is the move that protects both the lesson and the kid?
reviewCards.back: Praise something specific and true about how he set the problem up, then point at the step itself as the thing to revisit, not at him. Let him find the error in the work so he can correct it without admitting defeat to his parent.

reviewCards.front: A long-tenured employee has to be moved off a leadership role after an audit. You have an hour with her. What do you open with?
reviewCards.back: Open with a sentence she has said herself about the part of the work she loves most, then offer the new role as a fuller use of that strength. Hand her authorship of the change before the word demotion is ever spoken, so she walks out with a story instead of a wound.

reviewCards.front: A neighbor tells you, with confidence, a fact about your own profession that is plainly wrong. Three other neighbors are listening. What do you do?
reviewCards.back: Let it sit, or fold a corrected version into your next sentence as if you are agreeing and adding to it. Correcting him in front of the others guarantees you lose him, and usually the point. Save the precise correction for a private moment when his pride is not on the table.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Face-saving correction. The skill is handing someone a dignified way to change without making them admit they were wrong. Practiced enough, it becomes a reflex: before you correct, you look for the version of the truth the other person can carry out of the room and still stand up straight.

ifThenPlans.plan: If you are about to correct a teammate's mistake in a group chat or standup, then close the channel, walk over or DM them, and frame the fix as a process gap or unclear spec rather than their error.

If your partner or roommate did a chore wrong and you feel the urge to point it out, then first name one specific thing they did right about it, and only mention the change as a small tweak, not a verdict on their effort.
If you catch yourself drafting a message that proves someone wrong, then rewrite it so the other person could forward it to their mother without flinching, or do not send it.
If you are in a meeting where someone's bad idea is about to be voted down, then offer them a graceful pivot, asking which part of their idea you should keep, before the no lands.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one person you corrected in the last week, in writing or out loud, and send them a short note today that names something specific they got right in that same situation. No apology, no walk-back, just the praise you skipped.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, run a five-minute exit review before any hard conversation you have scheduled. Write down what the other person will have to carry home if it goes badly, then write the sentence that gives them a way to change without wearing the mistake. Bring that sentence into the room.

memorableLines.text: Correct a man in front of his crew and you have not fixed the plate, you have lost the cook by Monday.
memorableLines.why: The metaphor reverses what fixing actually means—fixing the behavior comes second to keeping the person, a turn that reframes the whole chapter.

memorableLines.text: Flatten her, and she will fight you for years. Hand her a story she can live inside, and she will take the change.
memorableLines.why: The contrast between two outcomes cuts away everything else and shows why the method matters—the person you need to keep is more important than being heard.

memorableLines.text: What you give up is the public scoreboard. What you keep is the person, on Monday morning, still willing to learn from you.
memorableLines.why: Concrete and specific about the actual exchange—pride for loyalty—with 'Monday morning' grounding the long-term relationship in real time.

chapters.title: How to Spur People On to Success
chapters.hook: Name the two clean measures by their bar number, before the nine-year-old decides whether to keep playing.
chapters.counterintuition: Most readers think encouragement is a tone, a warm voice, a pat on the shoulder. It is not. Vague warmth registers as politeness and changes nothing; it is the specific, named detail, said out loud before the person quits in their head, that decides whether they keep going.
chapters.reflectionBefore: Recall someone struggling at something you care about. When did you last tell them they were improving?
chapters.reflectionAfter: What's one small improvement you could praise in someone trying hard right now, before they give up?
chapters.keyTakeaway: Name the smallest real win out loud and specific, the brunoise cubes, the grandfather paragraph, before any correction; people only hear notes once they know you saw the good thing.

breakdown.fastRead:
A nine-year-old works through a Clementi sonatina at the kitchen piano. The left hand is a mess. But bars seven and eight are clean. In tempo, no rush.

Most teachers would start with the mess. Do not. Stop him, look him in the eye, and say, "Bars seven and eight, you nailed those." Watch his shoulders drop an inch. Now he can hear the rest.

Nobody works harder for the person who only saw what they got wrong.

Praise first, by name, and mean it. The correction can wait an hour.
breakdown.deepRead:
A line cook is in his third week. His chiffonade still looks like lawn clippings. But at family meal he turned out a tray of brunoise any French cook would respect, even cubes, no mush. The sous chef saw it happen.

The wrong move is to walk over at service and say, "Your cuts are still uneven." The cook hears one thing: he is failing. By Tuesday he is gone, and the line is short a body on a Friday night.

Try the other way. Wait for the lull. Say it loud enough for the next station to hear. "That brunoise at family meal. Even cubes. Best on the line today." An hour later, quietly, you mention the chiffonade.

Same feedback, different order. People can hear correction once they know you saw the good thing. Skip that step and every note you give sounds like proof you wrote them off a week ago.

This is not a compliment sandwich. A sandwich is a trick, and the cook smells it coming and braces. Real appreciation is specific. It names the brunoise, the cubes, the meal. "Good job" is a sandwich. "Even cubes at family meal, best on the line" is a fact.

Try it on a teenager who hands you a fourth draft of his college essay. The opening wanders. The closing is thin. But one paragraph about his grandfather's hands lands. Read that paragraph back to him in his own words. Tell him what worked before you turn the page.

Do it and he will keep handing you drafts. Skip it and senior year goes quiet.
breakdown.fullRead:
A charge nurse at a hospice has watched a new aide freeze twice. A patient's daughter cried in the hallway, and the aide left the room. The next day, a son broke down by the bed, and the aide stepped out again. On the third visit, something different. The aide stayed. She did not say a word. She just sat through it.

Most people in that job quit within ninety days. The charge nurse knows this, and she knows what it costs a family to be handed a stranger every week. So at the end of shift, in the break room, she does not say, "You're getting better." She says, "That third visit, when Mrs. Alvarez's husband was crying, you stayed. You kept your hands still and you stayed. That is the work." No qualifier. No but-clause. No mention of the first two times.

The aide cries a little. Then she comes back Friday.

Notice what the charge nurse did not do. She did not soften it with "I know the first two were rough." She did not hedge with "You're improving." She named one moment, by patient and by behavior, and stopped talking. The aide did not need encouragement. She needed evidence that someone saw her stay. "You stayed" is evidence. "You're doing great" is noise.

The move is this. Find the smallest real improvement, say it plainly, and say it before the person has decided whether to keep trying. The window is short. People decide to quit in private, on the drive home, in the parking lot. By the time they tell you, the decision has already set. Catch them while they are still asking the question.

A regional sales manager has a rep on the edge of a performance review. Forty calls listened to, thirty-nine bad. But on call twenty-two, around minute four, the rep finally stops pitching and asks the customer a real question. The customer talks for ninety seconds. The manager could open Monday's meeting with the thirty-nine. He plays the question instead. He says, "That. That right there is the move. Not the close. The question." The rep writes it down. The next week he does it twice.

The principle holds across rooms. A swim coach has eight adults in the lane, including a woman in her forties who has been afraid of the deep end for thirty years. Yesterday she let go of the wall for two seconds. At the end of class, with the others still in the water, the coach calls out, "Karen, those two seconds. I saw it. That was the hardest thing anyone did in this pool tonight." Karen comes back Tuesday. She would not have.

Praise that is not specific is heard as flattery, and flattery makes people trust you less, not more. "Great job" is empty. "Karen, those two seconds, I saw it" cannot be faked, because you had to be paying attention to say it. The whole point is that the person knows you watched.

Save praise for what is real. If the brunoise was mush, do not call it clean. People can tell. They will discount everything you say after, including the corrections you actually need them to land.

Find the two seconds, say them out loud, and say them before she dries off and decides not to come back.

examples.title: Leontyne hears two clean bars in a botched Clementi

planSpec.domain: a piano teacher working with a nine-year-old who botched the left hand of a Clementi sonatina but landed two measures cleanly
planSpec.audience: a private music teacher dreading the parent's question about progress
planSpec.stakes: whether the child quits lessons by spring or stays with the instrument long enough to love it
planSpec.requiredBeat: the teacher pauses on the two clean measures, names them specifically by bar number, and watches the child's posture change before saying anything about the rest

examples.scenario: On a Thursday at 4:15, Leontyne sits at the upright next to Wystan, age nine, who has just finished the Clementi sonatina with a left hand that wandered through three wrong chords. His shoulders are pulled up around his ears. His mother is in the waiting room with her coat already on. Leontyne is about to open her mouth, and she has to decide what the first sentence out of it will be: a gentle correction about the bass line, or something else entirely, because she heard bars 14 and 15 land cleanly under his small hand and she is not sure he heard himself do it.
examples.whatToDo: Stop. Say, 'Bars fourteen and fifteen, the left hand was right under the right hand, exactly together.' Then wait. Watch his shoulders. Only then talk about the rest.
examples.whyItMatters: A nine-year-old decides whether he is a kid who can play piano in the first ninety seconds after he stops playing. Naming a real success by bar number proves you were listening, and proof outranks praise.

examples.title: Dario Catches Jin's Brunoise Before the Chiffonade

planSpec.domain: a line cook on his third week being told his knife cuts are still uneven, except for the brunoise he turned out at family meal
planSpec.audience: a sous chef who was trained by yelling and is trying not to repeat it
planSpec.stakes: whether the cook quits before his fourth shift or stays and becomes the station's most reliable prep
planSpec.requiredBeat: the sous chef opens with the brunoise by name, in the kitchen where other cooks can hear, before mentioning anything about the chiffonade

examples.scenario: Dario steps onto the line at four-fifteen, before service, while two other cooks are breaking down cases at the next station. Jin has his head down at the board, already braced. Dario speaks loud enough that the prep cooks can hear. 'That brunoise you sent out at family meal. The carrot. Even cubes, every one of them. I checked. That was clean work.' Jin looks up. 'Yeah?' 'Yeah. Now, about the chiffonade.'
examples.whatToDo: Name the one cut the cook did clean, by the dish it went out on, where the rest of the room can hear it. Then, and only then, bring up the cut that still needs work.
examples.whyItMatters: Public, specific praise lands as proof the improvement got noticed. Proof is what a third-week cook needs to believe the work is worth showing up for tomorrow, before the criticism arrives.

examples.title: Sevda Names the Brennan Visit and Says Nothing Else

planSpec.domain: a hospice nurse coaching a new aide who froze the first two times a patient's family cried, then sat through it the third time without leaving the room
planSpec.audience: a charge nurse responsible for retaining aides in a job most people quit within ninety days
planSpec.stakes: whether a naturally gentle person believes she belongs in this work or transfers to billing by Friday
planSpec.requiredBeat: the charge nurse names the third visit specifically and tells the aide what she did right, with no qualifier and no but-clause attached

examples.scenario: In the hallway outside Room 4, after the family of the man with ALS has gone home, Sevda sets two paper cups of weak coffee on the medication cart and waits for Marsha to look up. Marsha is three weeks in and has already cleared her locker once this week. Sevda names the third visit out loud, the Brennan family, and tells her she stayed in the chair when the daughter cried. She stayed. That is what Sevda says, and nothing after it. No list of what to fix, no softening. Just the coffee cooling.
examples.whatToDo: Name the third visit by family out loud. Tell the aide what she did right and stop talking. Don't add a 'but' or a list of what to work on next.
examples.whyItMatters: A person learning hard work needs to hear that one true thing landed before she has bandwidth for what didn't. A 'but' resets the count to zero. The praise has to stand alone or it never registered.

examples.title: Yannick reads his son's fourth draft and finds the cedar paragraph

planSpec.domain: a father reading his teenage son's college application essay, the fourth draft, which is still uneven but has one paragraph about his grandfather that lands
planSpec.audience: a father who tends to fix things sentence by sentence and has watched his son stop showing him drafts
planSpec.stakes: whether the son ever asks for his father's help on the next essay or goes silent through senior year
planSpec.requiredBeat: the father reads the grandfather paragraph aloud back to his son and says exactly what worked in it before turning a page

examples.scenario: Yannick is at the kitchen table, fourth draft of Roan's college essay in front of him. He has been crossing out commas for two pages when he hits the paragraph about Roan's grandfather, the cedar shavings, the dust on his glasses. He reads it twice. He sets the pen down, reads the paragraph aloud back to Roan, and says, 'The cedar dust on his glasses is the only line in this essay that sounds like you.' His hand is on the corner of the page. He has to decide whether to turn it or stop here.
examples.whatToDo: Set the pen down. Read the paragraph that worked aloud back to him, name the exact line that did the work, and stop there. Save your marks for a later pass on the next draft.
examples.whyItMatters: A teenager who has watched three drafts come back bleeding will stop showing you the fourth. Naming what works first proves the reading was real, not a hunt for errors, so the next draft still arrives.

examples.title: Ferenc Plays Back the One Question That Wasn't a Pitch

planSpec.domain: a regional sales manager reviewing a struggling rep's call recordings and finding one call where the rep finally stopped pitching and asked a question
planSpec.audience: a regional sales manager about to put the rep on a performance plan
planSpec.stakes: whether the rep walks into next week believing he can sell or rehearses his resignation in the parking lot
planSpec.requiredBeat: the manager plays the one good question back to the rep and tells him that is the move, not the close, and watches the rep write it down

examples.scenario: Ferenc had the performance plan paperwork half-filled on his laptop. He'd queued nineteen call recordings from Anselmo, expecting nineteen versions of the same closing pitch. He found one outlier on the eighth call, minute four: Anselmo stopped mid-script and asked, 'What did the last vendor get wrong?' The buyer talked for six minutes. Friday, conference room B, Ferenc cues that clip and slides his phone across. 'That. Not the close. The question.' Anselmo reaches for a pen.
examples.whatToDo: Cue the exact clip, name the timestamp, and tell him plainly that the question is the move worth keeping. Then stop talking until he writes it down.
examples.whyItMatters: A rep who hears one specific thing he did right, named by the second on the tape, has something to repeat on Monday. A vague 'keep trying' gives him nothing to do at nine in the morning.

examples.title: Moira singles out the two seconds Edith let go of the wall

planSpec.domain: a swim coach working with a forty-year-old beginner who has been afraid of the deep end for thirty years and yesterday let go of the wall for two seconds
planSpec.audience: a recreation-center swim coach with eight adults in the lane
planSpec.stakes: whether the woman comes back next Tuesday or quietly cancels the rest of her sessions
planSpec.requiredBeat: the coach singles out the two seconds at the end of class, in front of the other adults, and says she saw it and what it meant

examples.scenario: At the lane edge, Moira watches Edith haul herself up the ladder and stand dripping with the towel pressed to her chest. The other seven adults are gathering kickboards. Moira knows what Edith will carry home: thirty years of staying out of deep water and another forty-eight minutes of mostly that. So she raises her voice for the lane to hear and says: yesterday, two seconds, you let go of the wall. That is the whole thing. That is the door. Edith looks up. Moira watches her decide whether next Tuesday exists.
examples.whatToDo: Name the two seconds out loud at the end of class, in front of the lane, before Edith leaves the deck. Tell her what she did and what it meant, no qualifier and no but-clause.
examples.whyItMatters: Edith's body forgets gains the moment she stands up. Praise has to land outside the pool, witnessed by the other adults, or the only thing she carries into Tuesday is the part she failed.

questions.prompt: A youth soccer coach has a ten-year-old who has missed every defensive assignment all season. In the last scrimmage, the kid tracked back once and broke up a counter. Practice ends in two minutes. What is the soundest move?
choices: Pull her aside, name the moment she tracked back to break the counter, and tell her that was real defense before saying anything else.
Wait until next practice to give a balanced summary so the praise does not feel like favoritism.
Lead with the missed assignments, since the praise will land harder once she knows the work she still owes.
questions.explanation: Specific, named appreciation lands first and opens the ear for correction later. Delaying it dilutes the moment, and leading with missed assignments tells her she has been written off and the rare good play did not register.

questions.prompt: A pottery instructor has a beginner whose first three bowls were lopsided, but the rim of the third was finally even and centered. The student looks ready to give up. What should the instructor say first?
choices: Three bowls in and your form is still off, but the next one will probably click.
The rim on that third bowl is centered and even. That is the hardest part of throwing, and you got it.
Most students take ten bowls to find their rhythm, so do not be discouraged.
questions.explanation: Naming exactly what worked, with the specific feature, gives the student something true to hold. The first option leads with deficiency, and the third offers vague reassurance that does not name a real win, so neither earns the next attempt.

questions.prompt: A manager tells her new hire, 'Great job today, but your reports still need work, and overall you are doing fine.' The hire seems to flinch. What is the underlying problem with the framing?
choices: She did not deliver the criticism early enough, so it lost its weight.
She mentioned the reports at all, which violates the rule of only giving positive feedback.
The praise is generic, the correction is wrapped inside it, and the hire smells the structure and braces for the real message.
questions.explanation: A vague praise-then-but pattern reads as a delivery vehicle for criticism, not as appreciation. The first option misreads the issue as timing. The second invents a no-criticism rule that does not exist; correction is fine, just not when it hijacks the praise.

questions.prompt: A driving instructor has a teen who has been weak on lane changes for six lessons. Today, on one merge, the teen finally checked the mirror and the blind spot in the right order. What should the instructor say at the next stoplight?
choices: On that merge by the on-ramp, you checked the mirror, then the blind spot, in the right order. That is exactly the sequence.
You did okay on that merge, but let's keep working on the others.
Nice merge. Now we should talk about your following distance and your speed control.
questions.explanation: Naming the specific merge, the specific sequence, and calling it correct gives the teen a concrete behavior to repeat. A vague 'okay' with a redirect blurs the win, and pivoting to other faults buries the one moment that proved he can do it.

questions.prompt: Two bakery managers see a new hire produce one neat lattice-top pie after a week of sloppy ones. Manager A says, 'Good work today.' Manager B says, 'That lattice on the apple pie. The strips are even and the weave is tight. That is the move.' Whose feedback is more likely to keep the hire trying?
choices: Manager A, because keeping praise short avoids embarrassing the hire in front of the team.
Manager B, because naming the lattice, the evenness, and the weave gives the hire something specific and true to repeat.
Neither is meaningfully different; the hire will hear them as the same encouragement.
questions.explanation: Specificity is what makes appreciation believable and repeatable. Manager A's line is generic enough to feel automatic. Saying both lines are equivalent ignores that one names a fact and the other could be muttered to anyone walking by.

questions.prompt: A team lead always opens reviews with two sentences of praise, then 'but,' then ten minutes of correction. After six months, his reports stop bringing him early drafts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: His reports have grown defensive and need coaching on how to receive feedback.
He should drop the praise entirely so the correction lands without confusion.
His praise has become a predictable preface to criticism, so it no longer registers as appreciation.
questions.explanation: A formulaic praise-then-but pattern trains the listener to wait for the real message and discount the opener. Blaming the reports inverts cause and effect. Dropping praise altogether removes the only thing that opens the ear for correction in the first place.

questions.prompt: A physical therapist is working with a stroke patient who has tried for three weeks to grip a pen. Today she held it for four seconds before it slipped. The session is ending. What is the right thing to say?
choices: You held that pen for four full seconds. Three weeks ago that was zero. That is the grip coming back.
Good effort. We will keep working on it next time.
Four seconds is a start, but we need to get to thirty before this is functional.
questions.explanation: Naming the four seconds and contrasting it with where she started turns a tiny win into evidence of progress. Generic encouragement does not register as real, and benchmarking against a far-off target makes the small gain feel like failure.

questions.prompt: A junior reporter files a draft. The lede is sharp. The middle wanders. The kicker is weak. The editor has ten minutes before deadline. What is the best opening move?
choices: Skip straight to the wandering middle so they have time to fix it.
Read the lede back to them out loud and say what makes it sharp before touching anything else.
Tell them the piece needs work and ask them to revise the whole thing.
questions.explanation: Named, specific praise on the strongest part earns the writer's attention for the cuts that follow. Skipping the praise sends the writer into revisions believing nothing worked. A vague 'needs work' tells them to start over without showing them what to keep.

questions.prompt: A barista trainer wants to understand why 'compliment sandwiches' usually fail to motivate new hires. Which best captures the reason?
choices: They take too long to deliver in a busy shop.
They violate a strict no-criticism rule that good trainers follow.
They are recognizable as a structure, so the listener braces for the criticism inside and discounts the praise as setup.
questions.explanation: The sandwich is a pattern people recognize, so the praise reads as packaging rather than as appreciation. Length is not the issue. There is no rule against criticism; the issue is that praise must be specific and freestanding to be heard as real.

reviewCards.front: A junior employee finally did one part of a task well, surrounded by parts that still need work. You want them to keep trying. What is the first move?
reviewCards.back: Praise the smallest real improvement out loud and by name, before the person decides whether to keep trying. Point at the specific thing that worked, in concrete terms (the bar, the cut, the paragraph), and let that land before any correction follows.

reviewCards.front: You catch yourself about to say 'good job' to a nervous new aide who finally stayed in the room during a hard moment. Why is that phrase the wrong tool, and what replaces it?
reviewCards.back: 'Good job' is generic, so the person hears reassurance, not evidence you saw them. Name the exact moment (the third visit, staying through the crying) and say what she did right, with no qualifier and no but-clause attached. Specifics prove you were watching.

reviewCards.front: A sales rep is one bad week from a performance plan. On a recorded call you hear him stop pitching and ask one real question. He has not heard from you yet. What do you do first, and why first?
reviewCards.back: Play that question back to him and tell him that is the move, before any feedback about closing or pipeline. People can hear correction once they know you saw the good thing first. Lead with the brunoise, name it, then the rest of the notes can land.

reviewCards.front: A friend says, 'I gave him a compliment sandwich and he still got defensive.' What is the diagnosis, and what would have worked instead?
reviewCards.back: A sandwich is a trick and people brace for the bread. Real appreciation is specific and stands alone: name one true thing the person actually did (the two clean measures, the even cubes, the grandfather paragraph) and let it sit before raising anything else. Specificity is what separates praise from a setup.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is naming, by specific detail, the one thing a person did better than last time, and saying it before you say anything else. Done well, it is not flattery and not a sandwich. It is a fact, said out loud, that proves you were watching.

ifThenPlans.plan: If you are about to give feedback on a draft, deck, or recording that has real problems, then before you open your mouth, find the one sentence or moment that genuinely improved over the last version and read it back word for word.

If your kid or partner hands you something they made and you can already see what is wrong with it, then point at the smallest specific thing that worked, name what it did, and stop talking before you reach for the rest.
If a workout buddy or a beginner you are coaching asks how they did and most of it was sloppy, then name the one rep, lap, or breath that looked clean, say which one and why, before you mention form.

If you finish a workout, writing session, or hard conversation and your first instinct is to list what went wrong, then stop and write down one specific thing you did better than last time, by detail, before you let yourself review the misses.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Tonight, pick one person you have been frustrated with this week. Write down on paper one specific true thing they did better recently than a month ago, with the detail attached, and tomorrow before noon say it to them out loud and then stop talking.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Every Friday afternoon, take ten minutes and go through your team or your household. Write one specific sentence about what each person did better this week than last, naming the moment by detail. Send the ones that fit, keep the rest, and watch how fast you start catching the small moves while they happen.

memorableLines.text: Nobody works harder for the person who only saw what they got wrong.
memorableLines.why: It articulates a truth about human motivation that readers sensed but couldn't name—that silence about what went right is worse than criticism.

memorableLines.text: People decide to quit in private, on the drive home, in the parking lot. By the time they tell you, the decision has already set.
memorableLines.why: Specific places reveal the hidden timeline of quitting and explain why named praise must arrive before that solitary moment of reckoning.

memorableLines.text: 'You stayed' is evidence. 'You're doing great' is noise.
memorableLines.why: This stark contrast crystallizes the whole chapter in four words; once you see generic praise as noise, you can't unsee it.

chapters.title: Give a Dog a Good Name
chapters.hook: Tell a man he is already careful with his things, within his hearing, and watch him spend the week proving you right.
chapters.counterintuition: Most people try to fix behavior by naming what is wrong with it, expecting the person to close the gap. The opposite move works better: name the better trait the person almost has, out loud, and let them quietly rearrange themselves to fit the name you gave them.
chapters.reflectionBefore: Think of someone you've labeled lazy or difficult. Hold that judgment about them.
chapters.reflectionAfter: What strength do they almost have? Name it, and watch how they start to live up to it.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Pick a flattering trait the person almost has, name it aloud where they can hear, and they will quietly close the small gap to match the better picture you handed them.

breakdown.fastRead:
A boss tells the kid at the next desk, loud enough for the floor to hear, that he is the most reliable man on the team. The kid is not. Not yet. By Friday he is in early, checking his own work, walking toward the name his boss handed him.

That is the whole move. Give a person a good name to grow into, and most of them try.

People rise toward the version of themselves you say out loud, faster than they will ever rise toward a list of corrections. Nobody wakes up hoping to be straightened out before lunch.

Name the better person they almost are, say it where they can hear, and step out of their way.
breakdown.deepRead:
A second-chair cellist slides in late again as the warm-up ends. The conductor does not sigh. He waits until the visiting soloist arrives that afternoon and says, in the cellist's hearing, "This is our most reliable opener." Her face does something small. The next Tuesday she is in her chair ten minutes early.

Nothing was corrected. Nobody was scolded. A name was placed on her, and she walked toward it.

Why does this work when nagging does not? People defend their own picture of themselves the way they bolt a front door. Tell a woman she is sloppy and the lock slides shut, even when the charge is fair. Hand her a flattering description that is almost true, and there is no door to lock. There is only a small gap to close, and closing it is easier than calling you a liar.

The whole thing sits on the word almost. You cannot invent a quality out of thin air. The cellist had, somewhere, the seed of being reliable: one rehearsal she nailed, one solo she did not flub. Find that seed and name it.

Try it on the snapping checkout clerk. You watched her one Tuesday, gentle with an older woman counting pennies. That is your seed. Slip her a note that says the older shoppers are starting to ask for her line. Skip the lecture about the other days. Hand her the better version and walk on.

Pick one true thing, say it where she can hear it, and let her rise.
breakdown.fullRead:
A father pours coffee for his brother at the kitchen table. The eleven-year-old is in the next room, half listening, the way boys do. The father says, low and matter of fact, "He's getting careful about his things lately. Found his cleats in the right bin yesterday." That is all. The uncle nods. The talk moves on.

The boy, who has not in fact been careful, hears it. Something in him registers. By Saturday his cleats are in the bin again. By the next week his books. Nobody has yelled. Nobody has made a chart. A name has been placed on him, quietly, where he could overhear it, and he has begun walking toward it.

This is the oldest move in the parent's playbook, and the manager's, and the husband's, and most of us have forgotten it. Name the better trait a person almost has, and let them rise to meet the name.

The head nurse on a cardiac ward knows this. Her newest charge nurse is sloppy on medication checks, and on a cardiac ward sloppy means somebody's mother gets the wrong dose. Three write-ups in, the woman is days from quitting or being fired. The head nurse tries one more thing. Before the next shift, where two other nurses can hear, she says, "She is the most careful documenter we have had in years. You should see her handoff notes." It is barely true. One shift last Thursday the notes were clean. That much is enough. The young nurse hears it. By the end of the month the documentation is, in fact, the best on the floor. Not because anyone corrected her. Because someone handed her a name worth keeping.

Why does it work? Nearly everyone carries two pictures of themselves: the person they are on a bad day, and the person they would be if things were going right. Criticism forces them to defend the bad-day picture, because defending it feels like survival. Praise of the good-day picture, said as if it were already true, leaves them nothing to fight. There is only the distance between the name and the truth, and closing that distance is easier than being exposed as a fraud.

The rule has edges. The name must be almost true. Tell the chronically late hire she is the most punctual in the office and she will laugh in your face. Tell her you noticed she opened up clean on Monday, and you have handed her something real to grow into. Pick the smallest true fact and build the name on it.

The other edge is timing. Say it before any correction, not after. A name placed after a scolding sounds like a bandage. Said first, with no agenda showing, it lands as a description of who the person already is. The husband who overhears his wife tell her sister that he has been patient lately will spend the next month being quietly more patient, and the two of them will never have to sit down for the talk.

Find the one true thing about the better person they almost are, say it where they can hear it, and step back. Most of them will walk toward the name they have been given. The ones who will not were never going to be moved by a lecture anyway.

examples.title: Ingvar names the new charge nurse careful before her shift

planSpec.domain: a head nurse on a cardiac ward describing a sloppy new charge nurse to her face as 'the most careful documenter we've had in years' before the next shift
planSpec.audience: a charge nurse two years into management who keeps losing staff she has corrected
planSpec.stakes: whether the new hire stops cutting corners on med reconciliation or quits within the month after another write-up
planSpec.requiredBeat: the head nurse picks one true sliver of carefulness already visible in the new hire and names her by it before any correction lands, and the new hire is shown adjusting her own behavior to fit the name

examples.scenario: Ingvar, head nurse on the cardiac ward, watches the new charge nurse, Brigitta, hand off at 6:58 a.m. Brigitta has been sloppy with med reconciliation all week and a write-up is already drafted. But last Tuesday Brigitta caught a duplicate heparin order nobody else flagged. As the night team gathers, Ingvar says, loud enough for Brigitta to hear, 'Brigitta is the most careful documenter we've had in years. Watch how she logs the heparin holds.' Brigitta's pen, halfway to her pocket, stops. She sits back down and opens the chart again.
examples.whatToDo: Pick one true sliver of carefulness she has already shown, name her by it in front of her peers, and let the correction wait until she has tried on the name.
examples.whyItMatters: People defend the self-image already on file. Hand them a flattering one that is partly true, and they spend their effort earning it instead of fighting you for the old one.

examples.title: Ms. Pendergast names Constanza in the soloist's hearing

planSpec.domain: a high school orchestra conductor introducing a chronically late second-chair cellist to a visiting guest soloist
planSpec.audience: a music teacher at a public school with no leverage beyond words
planSpec.stakes: whether the cellist starts arriving at warm-up or the section drifts further out of tune for the spring concert
planSpec.requiredBeat: the conductor introduces the cellist by a reputation she has not yet earned ('our most reliable opener') in the soloist's hearing, and the cellist's face shifts as she registers the name being placed on her

examples.scenario: Ms. Pendergast spots the visiting soloist, Mr. Beltran, in the doorway of the band room just as Constanza shoves through the side door, ten minutes late, hair still wet from the rain. 'Maestro, come meet Constanza,' Ms. Pendergast says, steering him over. 'She's our most reliable opener. Has the section tuned before the rest of us put our coffee down.' Mr. Beltran nods, pleased. Constanza's mouth opens. It closes. She sets down her case, sits, and pulls out her tuning fork without a word.
examples.whatToDo: Introduce her in the soloist's hearing by the small virtue she could grow into, then walk away before she can argue it. Let the name she just heard become the deal she keeps with herself.
examples.whyItMatters: A reputation handed to someone in front of a witness she respects becomes a quiet debt she pays back in behavior. Correction asks her to defend her old self. A name lets her start being a new one.

examples.title: Atticus Names His Son Careful While Pouring His Brother's Coffee

planSpec.domain: a father at the kitchen table speaking about his eleven-year-old son's messy room within the son's hearing while pouring coffee for a visiting uncle
planSpec.audience: a parent of a preteen who has tried nagging and lost
planSpec.stakes: whether the boy starts picking up after himself without a fight, or the family settles into another year of weekend yelling
planSpec.requiredBeat: the father refers to the boy, casually and without performance, as someone who is becoming careful about his own things, and the boy overhears it and the room records what he does next without telling us what to feel

examples.scenario: Atticus pours coffee for his brother at the kitchen table. Down the hall, his son Jasper's door is half open, the floor still littered with hoodies and a cracked retainer case. Atticus does not lower his voice. 'Jasper's been getting careful about his good things lately. Folded that jersey his grandfather gave him without anyone asking.' He slides the sugar across. The footsteps in the hall pause, then start again, slower. A drawer opens. The hoodie draped on the chair by his door is gone before the uncle leaves.
examples.whatToDo: Within the boy's hearing, name him by the better trait he is almost showing, citing one true small instance. Do not announce it to him. Do not follow up. Let the name find him.
examples.whyItMatters: A child given a quiet reputation to live up to can reach for it without surrendering. Nagging asks him to admit you were right; an overheard description hands him a role he gets to grow into on his own terms.

examples.title: Wilbur Rewrites the Note to Doreen at Register Six

planSpec.domain: a regional grocery manager writing a one-paragraph note to a checkout clerk known for snapping at customers
planSpec.audience: a manager of forty hourly employees who cannot afford to fire the clerk
planSpec.stakes: whether the clerk's Saturday shift produces another customer complaint or whether her line becomes the one regulars choose
planSpec.requiredBeat: the before note is the corrective version the manager almost sent; the after is the version that names the clerk as 'the one our older shoppers ask for' on the strength of one true Tuesday interaction, and we see what arrives in his inbox a week later

examples.scenario: Wilbur runs four stores in the river district and has known Doreen at register six for nine years. Tuesday a customer wrote in: Doreen had carried her bag of cat litter to the parking lot in the rain. Wilbur's first draft reads, 'Doreen, the snapping at customers has to stop. Final warning.' He saves it to drafts. He starts over. The second note begins, 'Doreen, you are the one our older shoppers ask for. Mrs. Coyle wrote in about Tuesday.' He clips it to her schedule. A week later his inbox holds two notes from regulars asking when Doreen works.
examples.whatToDo: Throw out the corrective draft. Find the one true Tuesday moment that already shows the trait you want more of, and name her by it in a single sentence she will keep.
examples.whyItMatters: People rise toward the name placed on them. A reputation she has not quite earned becomes a target she can hit, while a corrective note becomes a verdict she spends the week defending against.

examples.title: Isadora at the lectern, choosing what to call her client

planSpec.domain: a public defender preparing a teenage client for a sentencing hearing where the judge has already read the file
planSpec.audience: a lawyer who knows the judge will be looking for a reason to be lenient or harsh
planSpec.stakes: whether the boy walks out with probation or with eighteen months in a youth facility
planSpec.requiredBeat: the lawyer must choose between defending the client against the file's worst readings or standing up and naming the client by a quality the judge has not yet seen evidence of, and the lawyer commits to the second move knowing the client will hear himself described that way for the first time

examples.scenario: Isadora has the file open on the lectern. Three pages of incidents, two suspensions, one fight in a parking lot. The judge has read all of it and is waiting. Her client, sixteen, sits behind her in a borrowed shirt that does not fit at the collar. She has ninety seconds of remarks before sentencing. She can spend them arguing the file down, page by page, or she can stand up and tell the judge that the boy behind her is the one in his family who keeps showing up. Both are partly true. She has to pick one in the next breath, knowing the boy will hear whichever she chooses.
examples.whatToDo: Stand up and name him by the quality you want the judge to look for. Say it plainly, in his hearing, then sit down before the room can argue with the name.
examples.whyItMatters: The judge is searching the room for a person, not a file. A name placed on the boy gives the judge somewhere to land leniency, and gives the boy a self to grow into on the way out the courthouse door.

examples.title: Genevieve Notices What She Named Her Husband

planSpec.domain: a long-married woman writing in her journal about how her husband answers the phone now compared to a year ago
planSpec.audience: a spouse trying to repair a marriage without sitting her partner down for a 'talk'
planSpec.stakes: whether the daily texture of the marriage softens or the couple drifts into separate rooms permanently
planSpec.requiredBeat: the woman traces back to one specific evening she described her husband to her sister as patient, in his hearing, and she notices on the page that he has been quietly trying to be that man ever since, without either of them naming the deal

examples.scenario: Genevieve sits at the kitchen table at half past ten, her tea cold, the journal open. She is trying to remember when her husband stopped sighing into the phone. She traces it back to a Sunday last year, her sister at the sink with her, him answering a contractor's call in the next room. She had said, plain as pouring water, 'He is the patient one of us, you know.' He heard her. She is sure of it now. He has been working at being that man ever since, and neither of them has ever said so out loud.
examples.whatToDo: Find one true, generous word for your spouse and use it about him in his hearing, then let him try to live up to it without ever telling him you noticed.
examples.whyItMatters: A name spoken to a third party lands harder than any direct compliment, because it sounds like a private verdict the speaker did not know was being overheard.

questions.prompt: A new café owner has read about giving employees 'a good name' and is sketching how she will use it with her three baristas this Monday. Which description captures the move most accurately?
choices: Find a trait the person already shows in full and praise them loudly for it whenever they display it.
Invent a flattering label about the person and use it consistently until repetition makes them grow into it.
Name a slightly better version of who the person almost is, anchored in one true sliver of evidence, so they have a name to live up to.
questions.explanation: The move points just ahead of where the person already is, anchored in something real so the label is not flattery. Praising a trait already in full does not pull anyone forward, and inventing a label with no evidence reads as manipulation and breaks trust.

questions.prompt: A youth soccer coach has a forward who keeps shooting from impossible angles instead of passing. The team is losing close games. A guest scout is watching practice tomorrow. What is the soundest move?
choices: After practice, walk her through the three games where she failed to pass and ask her to commit to changing.
In the huddle, with the scout listening, name her as the unselfish playmaker the squad is becoming, then run a passing drill.
Bench her for the first half of the next game so she feels the cost of her selfishness.
questions.explanation: Naming her as the unselfish playmaker, in the scout's hearing, hands her a reputation worth deserving in the next drill. Listing her failures fixes her self-image as a ball hog, and benching teaches resentment rather than the instinct to pass.

questions.prompt: A tech lead notices that a junior developer keeps merging code without writing tests. The lead wants to apply the 'name the better trait' approach. What works best?
choices: Configure the repository to block any merge that lowers test coverage and let the tooling do the correcting.
Send her a private message reminding her that test coverage is required and that she has been falling short.
At standup, mention that she is becoming the teammate others trust to leave the codebase safer than she found it, and ask her to demo her coverage on Friday.
questions.explanation: The standup mention names her as the careful teammate and the Friday demo gives her a stage to deserve the name. A merge block treats her as a problem to route around, and a private warning makes her cautious rather than proud of leaving good work behind.

questions.prompt: A library volunteer coordinator has a retired man who is reliable but speaks brusquely to the kids in the children's section. Several parents have noticed. What is the soundest move?
choices: Introduce him to the Friday story-time crew as the volunteer the youngest readers warm up to fastest, then ask him to greet them at the door.
Quietly reassign him to the back stacks where he will not interact with families.
Sit him down with the parent complaints and ask him to soften his tone going forward.
questions.explanation: Naming him as the volunteer kids warm up to gives him a part to play the next time a child approaches the desk. Reassigning him to the stacks punishes without teaching the warmth, and reading him the complaints puts him on the defensive before he has tried.

questions.prompt: A construction foreman has an apprentice carpenter who leaves tools scattered across the site at the end of every shift. The crew is fed up. What is the soundest move?
choices: While the site supervisor is visiting, mention that the apprentice is shaping up to be the most organized hand on the crew, citing how cleanly he staged yesterday's framing.
Dock his pay for the time the crew loses searching for tools at the end of each shift.
Pull him aside in front of two senior carpenters and tell him plainly that he is the messiest worker on the crew.
questions.explanation: Naming him as the most organized hand, in the supervisor's hearing and tied to one real Tuesday, gives him a reputation he will quietly work to deserve. Docking pay sparks resentment, and shaming him in front of seniors fixes 'the messy one' as his identity on the crew.

questions.prompt: A principal told a chronically tardy teacher at a staff meeting that he expects her to 'finally show some professionalism.' Six weeks later her arrival times are worse. What is the deepest reason the move backfired?
choices: Public correction in education settings is always less effective than a private one-on-one meeting.
He named her by the trait she was failing at rather than one she could rise to meet, so the label confirmed who she already was instead of pointing somewhere to grow.
She does not respect his authority and would have ignored any feedback he gave.
questions.explanation: A name only works as a pull when it points just past where the person already stands. 'Finally show some professionalism' reads as a verdict on her current self with nowhere to climb, while 'becoming the most reliable opener of the morning' would have given her somewhere to walk. Authority and venue are downstream of that.

questions.prompt: A regional manager praised a salesperson as 'one of the top closers in the territory' during the Monday huddle, when in fact she ranks near the bottom. She left visibly resentful. What is the issue?
choices: The named trait must already exist as one true sliver of evidence, however small. An unearned name reads as flattery, and the trust the move depends on collapses on contact with the leaderboard.
She is too cynical to respond to any kind of praise from leadership at this stage of her career.
Praise should never include comparisons to other employees because it always creates internal competition.
questions.explanation: Naming a trait works only when one honest example backs it up. Calling her a top closer when the leaderboard says otherwise insults her intelligence and burns the move for next time. Cynicism and comparison rules are not the cause: an honest reference to one strong call would have landed.

questions.prompt: A swim coach told a struggling distance swimmer she was 'becoming an elite-level competitor' right after she finished last at a regional meet. She rolled her eyes and skipped the next two practices. Why did the move fail?
choices: Athletes that age reject all coach praise as a developmental phase, and the timing did not really matter.
He should have benched her from the next meet so she would understand the seriousness of her finish.
Said in the moment of the loss, the naming read as consolation for finishing last rather than recognition of something already real, like a strong split or a clean turn she could be proud of.
questions.explanation: A name placed on top of a fresh failure gets heard as a pep talk to soften the blow. The move requires pointing at a real sliver, like one strong 100 in the middle of the race, so the swimmer can recognize herself in the description. Benching teaches shame; the rejection theory excuses the coach.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit director has a board member who chronically misses meetings but brings strong donor connections. Which option is the soundest application of the principle?
choices: Send the full board the attendance roster with chronic absences highlighted in red so the social pressure does the work.
At the next gala, in the board member's hearing, mention that she has become the most dependable connector the board has, citing the introduction she made in March.
Stop inviting her to working sessions entirely and quietly use her only as a name on the donor solicitation list.
questions.explanation: Naming her as the most dependable connector at the gala, anchored in one real introduction, gives her a reputation to deserve at the next meeting. The highlighted roster shames her without offering a way up, and quietly sidelining her writes her off and forfeits the chance to change anything.

reviewCards.front: You need someone to change a habit you find sloppy. Before you correct them, what is the move this principle asks for?
reviewCards.back: Name the better trait the person almost has, then let them rise to meet the name you gave them. Find one true sliver of the quality you want more of, say it plainly within their hearing, and let the name do the pulling instead of the rebuke.

reviewCards.front: A checkout clerk on your team snaps at customers, but on Tuesday you watched her walk an older shopper to aisle nine. You sit down to write her a note. What goes on the page?
reviewCards.back: Skip the corrective draft. Write the version that names her as the clerk your older shoppers ask for, on the strength of that Tuesday walk. The accurate seed of praise gives her a reputation she will quietly start protecting, which the warning never would.

reviewCards.front: Your eleven year old will not pick up his room and nagging has stopped working. A relative is coming over for coffee. How do you use the visit?
reviewCards.back: While pouring coffee, mention to the relative, casually and without performance, that the boy is becoming careful about his own things. Let him overhear it and do not follow up. You have placed a name on him that he can now grow into without losing face to you.

reviewCards.front: You are defending a teenager at sentencing. The judge has read a file full of the boy's worst moments. You can rebut the file or you can do something else. What is the harder, better move, and why does it work even on a judge?
reviewCards.back: Stand up and name the client by a quality the file has not shown yet, in language the boy himself will hear for the first time. The judge gets a reputation to test against the sentence she is about to hand down, and the boy gets a name to start trying to deserve. Defending line by line only argues inside the file's frame.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You are practicing the skill of naming the better version of someone before they have fully earned the name, then trusting them to grow into it. It is a small act of public faith that costs you nothing and gives the other person a self-image worth defending. Done well, it replaces the hours you used to spend correcting with one true sentence said in front of a witness.

ifThenPlans.plan: If you are about to write a corrective note to someone on your team, then first find one real moment from the last two weeks where they showed the trait you wish they had more of, and open the note by naming them as the kind of person who does that.

If you catch yourself about to remind your partner of a habit you wish they would change, then instead, in earshot of a friend or family member, mention the version of that habit they already do well and stop talking.
If your child or younger sibling overhears you on the phone, then describe them to the person on the other end by the trait you most want them to grow into, and let them hear it without comment.

If you are introducing a volunteer or a new neighbor to a third person, then introduce them by the contribution you hope they will make, not the one already on their resume, and watch what they do next.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Today, pick one person you have been quietly disappointed in and write down one true sliver of the better trait you wish they had more of. Tomorrow, in front of at least one other person, refer to them by that trait, in a single plain sentence, and then change the subject.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, on the same day, look at the three people whose behavior is costing you the most patience. For each one, write down the name you would like to give them, the small true evidence that backs it up, and the witness you will say it in front of. Spend the rest of the week saying those names out loud where they can hear, and keep notes on what shifts.

memorableLines.text: Nobody wakes up hoping to be straightened out before lunch.
memorableLines.why: A humanizing observation that captures why correction fails, voiced with unexpected humor and grounded in the reader's own experience.

memorableLines.text: There is only the distance between the name and the truth, and closing that distance is easier than being exposed as a fraud.
memorableLines.why: Reveals the hidden psychology that makes the technique work—the reader realizes people choose self-improvement over admitting you were right about them.

memorableLines.text: Tell a man he is already careful with his things, within his hearing, and watch him spend the week proving you right.
memorableLines.why: Demonstrates the mechanic in concrete, specific language with an immediate visible result that shows the principle working in real time.

chapters.title: Make the Fault Seem Easy to Correct
chapters.hook: Tell a child she missed one measure, not that she cannot play, and watch her sit back down at the piano.
chapters.counterintuition: Most people think honesty means naming the full size of the problem. It does the opposite of what you want. A fault described as small and near at hand gets fixed; the same fault described as a character flaw gets defended, and the person walks away from the instrument, the job, or the class entirely.
chapters.reflectionBefore: Think of the last time you gave someone critical feedback. What was their first reaction?
chapters.reflectionAfter: Replay that moment. If you had described the gap as something they were already halfway to fixing, how would the conversation have gone differently?
chapters.keyTakeaway: Show people the gap between where they are and where you want them as one small, specific, near-at-hand adjustment they are already most of the way toward making.

breakdown.fastRead:
Annie tells her band director she is quitting trumpet. She has rushed the same two bars for weeks. He sits down beside her stand. "You play it right with the metronome," he says. "The timing is already in you. It just slips in those two bars." She tries again. She nails it.

People fix what feels small and almost done. They quit what feels like proof they are no good. So shrink the gap before you name it. Hand them a one-inch correction, not a rebuild, and they will reach for it before bed. Nobody starts a climb at bedtime.
breakdown.deepRead:
In a bakery at four in the morning, an apprentice named Daniel stands over a torn sheet of laminated dough and goes quiet. He has done this twice this week. The hotel order is due at six. The head baker walks over and does not say what most of us would say.

"It is not your hands," he says. "It is the butter. Look here, where it got too warm before the third fold. Same thing happened to me last Tuesday." He shows him the exact spot where the temperature went wrong, and how to feel it next time.

Notice what he did not do. He did not call Daniel sloppy. He did not lecture him on focus. He named one thing Daniel had already done right an hour earlier, the first two folds, and pointed only at the spot that went sideways.

When you want someone to change, make the gap between where they stand and where you want them small, specific, and close at hand. Not "you have a problem with timing." Two bars rush. Not "you are bad at algebra." Four sign errors on the back page.

The mind reaches for what it can grasp. Tell a person the correction is a one-inch lift and they will try it tonight. Tell them the correction is who they are, and they will go home and check whether the course is still droppable on Friday.

Hand them the smallest honest version of the gap, and they will cross it before the kitchen light goes out.
breakdown.fullRead:
A community college math instructor sits at her desk on a Thursday evening with a stack of midterm exams. One belongs to a man who works two shifts a week and has told her, twice, that he is bad at algebra and probably should not have come back to school at his age. His score is a 47.

She reads it carefully. The concepts are right. He set up every problem the way she taught him. He lost the points on sign errors, four of them, the same kind of mistake she has seen a thousand times. If she writes 47 on the front and a note that says "study harder, see me at office hours," he will drop the course on Friday and lose his financial aid for the term. He has a daughter in second grade who watches him do homework at the kitchen table.

She circles the four sign errors. In the margin she writes, "Your algebra is right. These are sign flips, the most common kind. We can clean this up in twenty minutes Monday."

He shows up Monday.

The instinct, when someone falls short, is to name the size of the failure. To say it plainly, so they take it seriously. The instinct is wrong. People do not respond to the size of the gap. They respond to whether the gap looks like a step or a climb. Call it a climb, and they will look for a different hill, or no hill at all. Call it a step, with their foot already half lifted, and they will take it.

Watch how this works in three other places. A swim coach with a forty-six-year-old learner who keeps lifting his head to breathe says, "It is a one-inch fix. Your rotation, the hard part, is already right." A hardware store manager with a cashier whose drawer keeps coming up short says, "I watched you handle that split tender flawlessly yesterday. The only thing missing is the recount before close, which I have seen you do every Saturday." A father whose daughter has decided she cannot play piano in front of people says, "You missed one measure in a piece you have played right forty times. Start your practice from bar nine this week and let us see what happens Wednesday."

In each case the correction is small, named, and sitting next to something the person has already done right. None of this is flattery. The swim coach is not lying about the rotation. The manager really did watch the split tender. The father really did count the correct repetitions. The aim is not to soften the truth. The aim is to hand the person the smaller, true version of it, the one that fits in the hand.

Most correction fails because it sets the cost of changing higher than the cost of staying the same. A person who believes the fix is a rebuild will not start tonight. A person who believes the fix is four sign errors, a one-inch lift, a single missed measure, will start tonight, before their nerve fails them.

So before you correct anyone, do the work yourself. Find the smallest honest way to describe the gap. Find the thing the person has already done right that proves the gap is crossable. Say that part first, by name, before you mention what is missing. The fault is not who they are. It is one step from where they already stand. Tell them so, and they will take it tonight, before the kitchen light goes out.

examples.title: Marek's Three Minutes at Lotte's Locker Before Homeroom

planSpec.domain: a high school band director correcting a trumpet player who keeps rushing the tempo in the second movement
planSpec.audience: a teacher who has watched the student practice alone and knows she actually has the timing
planSpec.stakes: whether the trumpet player gives up before the spring concert and quits band entirely, which she has been threatening since October
planSpec.requiredBeat: the director points out that the rushing only happens in two measures and that her metronome work last week proves the timing is already in her hands

examples.scenario: Marek stands alone in the band room at 3:47 Thursday, chairs still fanned from rehearsal, the second-movement score open on his stand. Lotte packed her trumpet and walked out saying again she is done, the spring concert can go on without her. He heard her play this same passage clean against a metronome last Wednesday. Tomorrow he has three minutes at her locker before homeroom. He is about to mark the two measures, only two, where she rushes, and write the metronome marking she already nailed.
examples.whatToDo: Circle the exact two measures she rushes, then point to last Wednesday's metronome session and tell her plainly: the timing is already in her hands, this is a two-bar fix, not a rebuild.
examples.whyItMatters: A student one foot out the door cannot hear feedback that sounds like a verdict on her ability. Naming the gap as small and already half-closed turns the fix into a next step instead of a confession of failure.

examples.title: Sabine Catches the Tear at Four A.M. With Yusuf

planSpec.domain: a head baker training a new apprentice whose laminated dough keeps tearing during the final fold
planSpec.audience: a baker running a small shop with one hire and no time to redo a batch
planSpec.stakes: the morning's croissant order for a hotel client who pays for thirty laminated pieces by 6am
planSpec.requiredBeat: the baker tells the apprentice that the tear is a butter-temperature problem he has already solved twice this week, not a hands problem, and shows him where the chill went wrong

examples.scenario: At 4:12 a.m. in Sabine's two-person bakery, the third sheet of dough splits at the final fold. Her apprentice Yusuf is staring at the marble like it has betrayed him. 'I'm sorry, my hands are wrong, the third turn keeps tearing.' Sabine shakes her head. 'It is not your hands. I tore one Tuesday and one Thursday, same fold, same shop. Look at the sheen on the butter, that is sweat, not chill. We pulled this block from the cooler four minutes too early. Put your finger on the seam and tell me what you feel.'
examples.whatToDo: Name the tear as a butter-temperature problem you have already hit twice this week, not a skill gap, then show him the warm patch and walk him through the four-minute chill that fixes it.
examples.whyItMatters: A new hire quits a craft when the fault looks like talent. Pinning the gap to a chill window he can actually hit puts the next croissant inside his reach and keeps the morning's batch on the hotel counter.

examples.title: Yashar Reaches for the Red Pen on Devontae's Midterm
